newsitem.title: UK: Severn leads water shares to record highs.
newsitem.headline: Severn leads water shares to record highs.

text.p: Stock shortages and continuing pre-budget confidence helped to squeeze Severn Trent and others in the water sector to new twelve-month highs on Wednesday.

The sharp gains in the sector came just hours before Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown was due to announce details of a one-off "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utility companies.
"People have been caught short of stock in the sector and the shares have been spurred on by thoughts that the Chancellor is going to be less aggressive than first feared," one senior dealer said.
Severn Trent was up 10-1/2p to 820-1/2p by 1111 GMT after peaking at a new twelve-month high of 845 in early trade.
Anglian Water notched up a year high of 747p before easing slightly to be up 12p at 705p, and South West Water rose to 764p, another twelve-month record, before paring gains to be up 15p at 744-1/2p.
But dealers commented that much of the hike in utility share prices had been defensive and trading volumes remained slim with prices exaggerated by market-makers attempting to keep positions flat.
The FTSE 100 index later shed all of its gains to be slightly down on the day as pre-budget nerves set in.

Water stocks had been bolstered by optimism over the level of the proposed "windfall tax" and analysts said the shares remained undervalued. Investors were hoping that the sector would still be able to return value to shareholders.

"The reality is that once the windfall tax is known there will be a number of share buy-backs and special dividends in this sector over the next few months..particularly among companies like Wessex Water and Severn Trent which have very strong balance sheets," said Nigel Hawkins, utilities analyst at Yamaichi.
Severn Trent has already said it will complete a 10-percent buyback of its shares.

Hawkins predicts the windfall tax will also be limited to around five billion stg with water stocks taking a 1.2 billion stg share. Some analysts had previously feared that the overall burden of the tax could amount to around seven billion stg.

"If the windfall tax is not so severe then these stocks will be off to the races," said one dealer. "But there's not a lot of room for error, and if they do whip them they'll come racing back down again."

Any instant abolition of ACT, the tax credit which some institutions can claim back on dividend payments, could also hit the sector hard, with United Utilities and Hyder among the more high yielding stocks.
"I expect ACT to be phased out over four years," Hawkins said. "Instant abolition would have a significant adverse market reaction."
